The 2017 Transformer did not emerge without predecessors. Its history combines attention mechanisms developed for neural machine translation, self-attention, sequence-to-sequence models, large-scale training, and different objectives across model families. This selective timeline highlights milestones; it is neither exhaustive nor a claim of a single causal path.

## Placing LLMs in the AI landscape

This classification helps distinguish **the kind of method** an LLM belongs to from **the problem domain** in which it is used. It complements the timeline; it is not a step in a model's computation.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph AI["Artificial intelligence"]
    subgraph ML["Machine learning"]
      subgraph DL["Deep learning<br/>(neural networks)"]
        LLM["LLM"]
      end
    end
  end
  NLP["NLP: a domain of problems<br/>(rules, statistics, models, LLMs…)"]
```

- **Deep learning** denotes a family of methods: neural networks with multiple layers. Current LLMs belong to it.
- **Natural language processing** (NLP) denotes a domain of problems: processing or producing language. It is addressed by very different methods — linguistic rules, statistical models, specialized systems, and neural networks. LLMs are a dominant but not exclusive answer: a production system can combine rules, specialized models, document retrieval, tools, and LLMs.
- The term **LLM** has no universal numerical threshold: it generally refers to language models trained at large scale, using substantial data and compute. The *foundation model* concept instead emphasizes reuse: a model serving as a base for many applications. The concepts are related, but they are not synonyms.

Dates distinguish submissions, announcements, and releases. Milestones are grouped by research area; chronological order does not imply a single causal chain.

## Which bottlenecks changed—and which remain

The timeline becomes more meaningful when we follow the problems researchers were trying to overcome. This is not a story in which each new architecture makes the previous one obsolete: each family addresses particular needs and retains trade-offs.

### 1. Recurrence: a dependency cost over time

In an RNN, the hidden state at position (t) depends on the state at (t-1). This imposes a computation order within an example: all positions cannot be computed simultaneously as though they were independent. It limits the parallelism available during training, especially for long sequences.

LSTMs and GRUs improved information flow and the learning of long-range dependencies; they did not remove the sequential dependency chain. Sequence-to-sequence models also used fixed-size states to summarize a sequence, which could become a bottleneck. Attention in neural machine translation let the decoder consult different parts of the source sequence rather than relying only on a single summary ([Bahdanau et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)).

### 2. 2017: changing the path of computation

The Transformer introduced by Vaswani et al. generalizes this idea by placing attention at the center of the architecture. In the encoder's central computation, positions can be processed in parallel: they interact through attention rather than through a chain of recurrent states. This structural change is particularly well suited to parallel accelerators ([Vaswani et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)).

The advance has its own costs. Dense attention compares positions with one another; in its standard form, its compute and memory costs grow quadratically with sequence length. And in an autoregressive GPT, the next token still depends on previous ones: *prefill* processes the prompt in parallel, but *decode* produces new tokens one at a time.

### 3. From task-specific models to reusable models

Transfer learning was a major historical shift: instead of designing an independent model for every task, learned representations and parameters could be reused across downstream tasks. Pretrained word representations, followed by contextualized pretrained models, prepared this change. GPT-2 illustrated the potential of zero-shot transfer; GPT-3 made it especially visible through few-shot evaluations in which tasks and demonstrations were supplied in the prompt, without gradient updates ([Brown et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)).

This history leads to several mechanisms that should now be distinguished rather than collapsed into one timeline:
- **Transfer with adaptation**: update parameters on a downstream task (*fine-tuning*).
- **Context-based adaptation**: provide instructions or examples without changing parameters (*zero-shot*, *few-shot*, ICL).
- **External knowledge supply**: retrieve information and transmit it to the model, for example through RAG; this is not parameter transfer.

Their mechanisms, conditions for success, and limitations are explored in [LLM evolution](llm-evolution.qmd) and [in-context learning](in-context-learning.qmd). [RAG and memory boundaries](rag-memory-boundaries.qmd) explain why retrieving information does not yet mean it is accessible to the model.

### 4. Scale, post-training, and observed capabilities

From the 2020s onward, progress was no longer only about architecture: model size, data quantity and quality, training compute, and optimization procedures became variables studied together. Scaling laws and compute-optimal allocation helped formalize these trade-offs ([Kaplan et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361); [Hoffmann et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)).

In parallel, post-training—especially instruction tuning and preference optimization—shaped pretrained models toward assistant-like behavior. Some capabilities also appear to emerge as scale increases, but interpretation depends on tasks and metrics: evaluation thresholds can make gradual progress look sudden ([Schaeffer et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004)). These topics are examined in [LLM evolution](llm-evolution.qmd), [scaling laws](scaling-laws.qmd), [emergence](emergence.qmd), and [post-training](post-training.qmd).

### What this history lets us conclude

The timeline highlights three mutually reinforcing but distinct transformations: the Transformer changes the path of computation; large-scale pretraining makes learned parameters reusable; later methods adapt a model through its parameters, through context, or by supplying external information. To compare generations and understand the dimensions evolving in parallel—multimodality, inference-time compute, efficiency, and tool-using systems—see [From GPT-2 to contemporary LLM systems](llm-evolution.qmd).

## What the timeline should not imply

- **Transformer does not mean autoregressive LLM.** The 2017 paper presents an encoder-decoder architecture for translation; BERT uses an encoder and a masked prediction objective.
- **Attention predates the Transformer.** The 2017 paper assembles and reorganizes existing ideas into a coherent architecture; it did not invent the entire family of attention mechanisms.
- **Scale does not explain everything.** Data, objectives, tokenization, architecture, training procedure, and evaluation also shape observed capabilities.
- **A publication date is not proof of absolute priority.** This page selects a few pedagogical milestones and does not attempt to catalogue every parallel contribution.
